claims.claim: Kay states that when writers work with distant history they are, to a great degree, guessing.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Home and Away', BrightWeavings (speech, amended; short version Globe and Mail 1999)
claims.quote: we are all guessing
claims.page: body, paragraph on The Lions of Al-Rassan and Rodrigo Diaz

claims.claim: Kay says inventing a setting and a character modelled on a real figure demonstrates a measure of appropriate distance.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Home and Away', BrightWeavings
claims.quote: a measure of appropriate distance

claims.feature: other: universalising by detaching from a named context
claims.claim: Kay claims that setting a story as fantasy detaches the tale from a narrow context.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Home and Away', BrightWeavings
claims.quote: It detaches the tale from a narrow context
claims.page: body, 'what can fantasy do better' section

claims.feature: other: honesty about the limits of historical knowledge
claims.claim: Kay argues that treating the past as fantasy is a way of being honest about limitations.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Home and Away', BrightWeavings
claims.quote: a way of being honest about limitations

claims.feature: other: escape that returns the reader home
claims.claim: Kay endorses Douglas Barbour's description of admired fantasy as the kind of escape that brings you home; the phrase is Barbour's, quoted by Kay.
claims.source: Douglas Barbour, quoted approvingly by Guy Gavriel Kay in 'Home and Away', BrightWeavings
claims.quote: The kind of escape that brings you home.

claims.feature: other: competing versions of one story
claims.claim: Kay asserts that all renderings of a legend matter and that the changes between versions carry truths about the societies that made them.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'On Myth' (Chapters 'Great Writers' series newspaper insert)
claims.quote: All renderings matter

claims.claim: Kay states that in the study of myth the earliest version of a legend is not always the most important.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'On Myth', BrightWeavings
claims.quote: the earliest version of a legend isn’t always the

claims.claim: Kay says he tried to write Tigana's themes in with a stiletto rather than a bludgeon, slipping them in quietly while keeping the reader turning pages.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Afterword to the ROC USA tenth anniversary edition of Tigana, reprinted on BrightWeavings
claims.quote: I tried to imagine myself with a stiletto not a bludgeon

claims.claim: Kay says he wanted to open a book about subterfuge and deception with an outright lie, and that the first sentence of chapter one does so.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Tigana Afterword (1999), BrightWeavings
claims.quote: start a book about subterfuge and deception with an outright lie
claims.page: paragraph on first sentence and music

claims.claim: Kay says the two Prague Spring photographs showed a functionary not only killed but made never to have been, and that this image lingered twenty years and seeded Tigana.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Tigana Afterword (1999), BrightWeavings
claims.quote: not only killed, but made to never have been

claims.claim: Kay states that names link to history and that a sense of history is needed to define ourselves.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Tigana Afterword (1999), BrightWeavings
claims.quote: Names link to history

claims.claim: Kay rejects the idea that fantasy is essentially about variations on hyphens and apostrophes in invented names.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'On Writing Sailing to Sarantium', written for Earthlight (UK publisher)
claims.quote: hyphens and apostrophes in invented names
claims.page: middle section on what fantasy is

claims.claim: Kay says he is happy establishing a space between the invented character and the real man on whom he is based.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Under Heaven Author's Letter, printed in the advance reading copies
claims.quote: a space between the invented character and the real man
claims.page: paragraph on the Tang prime minister

claims.claim: Kay says the shift from real China to an imagined Kitai serves notice that he reserves the right to change or telescope events.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Under Heaven Author's Letter (2010)
claims.quote: I reserve the right to change, or telescope events
claims.page: paragraph on keeping readers turning pages

claims.feature: other: accumulated detail as reader trust
claims.claim: Kay claims the quiet, steady accumulation of detail and complexity reaches readers almost subliminally and earns their trust in the book.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Rodger Turner for SFSite
claims.quote: the quiet, steady accumulation of detail
claims.page: answer on the 'credibility of the book'

claims.claim: Kay says what we know of the great figures of the past is shaped by, and at the mercy of, those who chronicled them, citing Procopius on Justinian and Theodora.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Rodger Turner for SFSite
claims.quote: at the mercy of!) those who chronicled them

claims.claim: Kay says a viewpoint character observing a setting for the first time serves as a window for the reader, so the character's initiation becomes the reader's.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Rodger Turner for SFSite
claims.quote: A viewpoint character who is observing a setting for the first
claims.page: answer on the 'fish out of water' technique

claims.claim: Kay says he does not deliver a book until it is close to where he wants it and is therefore very lightly edited across his three English-language publishers.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Rodger Turner for SFSite
claims.quote: so I’m very lightly edited

claims.claim: Kay says he likes to work with cross-sections of a culture or society and so tends to have figures from many different classes.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, quoted in Sandy Auden, 'A Question of Character', UK Sci Fi Channel website
claims.quote: cross-sections of a culture or society

claims.claim: Kay says he has been trying to offer the ambience or flavour of various times and places through the prism of fantasy.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, quoted in Sandy Auden, 'A Question of Character', UK Sci Fi Channel website
claims.quote: the ambience or flavour of various times and places

claims.claim: Kay says characters he thinks of as minor grow in importance because he likes their voice.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, quoted in Sandy Auden, 'A Question of Character', UK Sci Fi Channel website
claims.quote: grow in importance because I like their voice
claims.page: early in the article, on making characters

claims.claim: Kay says telescoping the Reconquista's three hundred years into effectively two generations lets him intensify the reader's response by keeping it with one set of characters.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Guy Haley, SFX #93
claims.quote: telescoping events into effectively two generations

claims.feature: other: research must be digested not dumped
claims.claim: Kay names as failed fiction writing the book in which great gobbets of raw fact are tucked in like an undigested meal.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by James Schellenberg and David M. Switzer, Challenging Destiny #11
claims.quote: great gobbets of raw fact are tucked into the book
claims.page: answer on balancing nonfiction and fiction

claims.claim: Kay says we remember the great figures of history fundamentally through what was written about them.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed for Challenging Destiny #11
claims.quote: Fundamentally through what was written about them
claims.page: answer on the Sarantine Mosaic's themes

claims.claim: Kay lists the unreliable narrator among the tools available to a writer, alongside dramatic irony, switching viewpoints, suspense and eroticism.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed for Challenging Destiny #11
claims.quote: dramatic irony, the unreliable narrator, switching viewpoints
claims.page: answer on writing in other genres

claims.claim: Kay says most people can only say 'I lived' through family transmission, instancing a grandson given a grandfather's name, an anecdote about Great-Uncle Henry, a recipe, an heirloom.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed for Challenging Destiny #11
claims.quote: an anecdote passed down through the family about Great-Uncle Henry
claims.page: answer on leaving a name that endures

claims.claim: Kay says it is irresponsible for a book that pitches its stakes high to resolve the conflict with no consequences or losses to the characters.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed for Challenging Destiny #11
claims.quote: no consequences or losses to the characters
claims.page: answer on putting characters in painful situations

claims.claim: Kay says writers treating history must be aware of their own prejudices and presuppositions and filter for them as best they can.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed for Challenging Destiny #11
claims.quote: filter for them as best you can

claims.feature: other: history as residue on ordinary lives
claims.claim: Kay says that in Sailing to Sarantium he wanted the protagonist to be less central to the great events and to examine how those great events impact ordinary lives.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, chat transcript, Event Horizon 'Flashpoint' hosted by Jim Freund
claims.quote: how those great events can impact on ordinary lives
claims.page: early in the transcript, on the premise

claims.feature: other: worldbuilding consistency as a game
claims.claim: Kay says Tolkien would have constructed an elaborate explanation for a map discrepancy as part of his worldbuilding game, and declines to do so himself.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, chat transcript, Event Horizon
claims.quote: as part of his worldbuilding
claims.page: answer to Ran on the maps in Lions and Sarantium

claims.feature: other: know the period before varying it
claims.claim: Kay says that a fantasy based on a period is a variation on a theme and that a writer has to know the theme before trying variations.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed for Deep Magic ezine
claims.quote: you have to KNOW the theme before you try variations

claims.feature: other: intuition described after the fact
claims.claim: Kay warns readers to be sceptical when writers present intuitive processes as thought-out planning, saying his own approach was an evolution he discovered rather than a strategy laid out in advance.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'On the Strengths of Fiction Done as Near-History', boingboing.net
claims.quote: be skeptical when writers present intuitive processes as thought-out planning

claims.feature: other: no dates or facts on the page
claims.claim: Kay names as a risk of his method that readers will never learn the year of the Treaty of Utrecht in his novels and will not have a desire to learn the real facts assuaged.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'On the Strengths of Fiction Done as Near-History', boingboing.net
claims.quote: Readers will never learn the year of the Treaty of Utrecht

claims.claim: Kay says of the historical reversal embodied in A Song for Arbonne that he tried to do it lightly and to let the reader go as far as he or she wanted down that road.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'On the Strengths of Fiction Done as Near-History', boingboing.net
claims.quote: I tried to do it lightly, to let the reader go
claims.page: body, A Song for Arbonne section

claims.claim: Kay says the Sarantine Mosaic let him develop thoughts about Procopius the historian and about the writers of history, chroniclers and artists.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'On the Strengths of Fiction Done as Near-History', boingboing.net
claims.quote: about the writers of history, chroniclers and artists

claims.claim: Kay says that in The Lions of Al-Rassan he wanted to explore interactions not ideologies.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'On the Strengths of Fiction Done as Near-History', boingboing.net
claims.quote: I wanted to explore interactions not ideologies

claims.feature: other: the reader completes the book
claims.claim: Kay says each reader makes the book they read.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'On the Strengths of Fiction Done as Near-History', boingboing.net
claims.quote: each reader makes the book they read
claims.page: body, A Song for Arbonne section

claims.claim: Kay says his main contribution to the discussion of writing advice is that there are no rules.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Some Writing Advice: Don't Take Others' Advice', LitHub
claims.quote: There are no rules

claims.claim: Kay cites, as an instance of the writing-advice industry he is allergic to, that people everywhere tell you not to use italics.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Some Writing Advice', LitHub
claims.quote: People everywhere tell you not to use italics

claims.feature: other: the past rhymes rather than repeats
claims.claim: Kay says he writes with the idea that history may not repeat but it rhymes, attributing the line to the psychoanalyst Theodore Reik rather than Mark Twain.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'The Big Idea', Whatever (John Scalzi's blog)
claims.quote: history may not repeat, but it rhymes
claims.page: body, on Written on the Dark

claims.feature: other: the past rhymes rather than repeats
claims.claim: Kay says the fantastic quarter-turn makes reader and author share that they are rhyming with the past, not trying to pin the present down with it precisely.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'The Big Idea', Whatever
claims.quote: rhyming with the past, not trying to pin the present down

claims.claim: Kay says he wants readers thinking about their own time but not for lessons, because he is offering a story and not giving a lecture.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'The Big Idea', Whatever
claims.quote: I’m offering a story not giving a lecture

claims.feature: other: meaning left to the reader
claims.claim: Kay says he is focused on complicating things, on nuance, and on letting readers decide what they find in or take away from a book.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'The Big Idea', Whatever
claims.quote: letting readers decide what they find in or take away from a book

claims.feature: other: no dates or facts on the page
claims.claim: Kay says being alert to the themes of history does not necessarily mean the minutiae of dates and places, but patterns, lessons and warnings.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Children of Earth and Sky Author Questions, BrightWeavings
claims.quote: the minutiae of dates and places

claims.claim: Kay says he believes in the need to vary the tension, the drama, the type of scenes a book has, and even the language in which the story is told.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Children of Earth and Sky Author Questions, BrightWeavings
claims.quote: vary the tension, drama, the type of scenes a book has

claims.claim: Kay says that if a book is done well readers can be moved by a single line about an artist becoming a sculptor of hands, because they know why he did that.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Children of Earth and Sky Author Questions, BrightWeavings
claims.quote: moved by a single line about an artist becoming a sculptor

claims.claim: Kay says artists are the recorders and chroniclers of a time and can become for later eras the emblems of a day.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Children of Earth and Sky Author Questions, BrightWeavings
claims.quote: the recorders, chroniclers of a time

claims.feature: other: history as residue on ordinary lives
claims.claim: Kay says Children of Earth and Sky was deliberately about people who are not important in the scheme of things, and about how grand events can reach down and affect people far away.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Children of Earth and Sky Author Questions, BrightWeavings
claims.quote: how those grand events can reach down and affect people far away

claims.claim: Kay says he declined a Fernand Braudel passage as an epigraph because it felt too on the nose as to one theme.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Children of Earth and Sky: An Origin Story', BrightWeavings
claims.quote: it felt too ‘on the nose’ as to one theme

claims.claim: Kay says he prefers epigraphs of association, ones that open up more after a reader has finished a book.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Children of Earth and Sky: An Origin Story', BrightWeavings
claims.quote: I prefer epigraphs of association

claims.claim: Kay says the Provence landmarks he stumbled on, among them a round roofless medieval watchtower in the middle of nowhere, started a different sort of tale telling itself to him.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Letter to the Reader of Ysabel'
claims.quote: a round, roofless medieval watchtower in the middle of nowhere

claims.feature: other: history as residue on a place
claims.claim: Kay says he began thinking about how some parts of the world still carry the hard imprint of what has gone before.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Letter to the Reader of Ysabel'
claims.quote: still carry the hard imprint of what has gone before

claims.feature: other: research must be digested not dumped
claims.claim: Kay says his grounding in research has to be so secure that the vast majority of it does not enter the book except subliminally or very quietly, or else the result is the info dump he hates as a reader.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Kristin Centorcelli, SF Signal
claims.quote: does not enter the book except subliminally, or does so very quietly
claims.page: answer on research for River of Stars

claims.feature: other: minor figures carry the setting
claims.claim: Kay says he often achieves his strongest effects through the peripheral figures, whether of character, emotion, or shaping depth to a setting for the reader.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Kristin Centorcelli, SF Signal
claims.quote: through the peripheral figures I can achieve my strongest effects

claims.claim: Kay says he uses what he calls the porter in Macbeth idea, holding back the revelation of something or the moving forward of the main plot, to heighten drama.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Kristin Centorcelli, SF Signal
claims.quote: holding back the revelation of something, or the moving forward

claims.claim: Kay says the principal reason the language of the Fionavar trilogy differs from his later books is that Fionavar was his mythic endeavour while the later books track a movement towards history.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Afterword to the HarperPerennial Canada 20th anniversary edition of The Fionavar Tapestry
claims.quote: The principal reason the language of the trilogy differs from my later books

claims.claim: Kay says the language of Fionavar was guided by the matter of the book, a god imprisoned under a mountain and a wolf and dog fighting beneath a sacrificial tree.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, The Fionavar Tapestry Afterword (2003)
claims.quote: Language was guided by that context

claims.claim: Kay says he imagined the narrative arc of Fionavar in operatic terms, moving from aria to aria.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, The Fionavar Tapestry Afterword (2003)
claims.quote: I imagined the arc of the narrative in operatic terms, moving from aria to aria

claims.claim: Kay says he has joked that the scale of Fionavar was built so that he could write the sentence 'Rain, rain, rain, rain, rain' for Paul on the Summer Tree.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, The Fionavar Tapestry Afterword (2003)
claims.quote: Rain, rain, rain, rain, rain.

claims.claim: Kay says he does not believe in saying exactly what happens to characters after a novel closes, and that the ending of every book he has written makes this point.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, The Fionavar Tapestry Afterword (2003)
claims.quote: I don’t believe in saying exactly what happens to characters after a novel closes

claims.claim: Kay says he cut a planned Sharra scene because it felt static and flat and was in the book only to tie up a thread he did not think was really loose.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, The Fionavar Tapestry Afterword (2003)
claims.quote: The scene felt static, flat

claims.claim: Kay says an exile experiencing a new place gives the reader a way in, because that character's observations and reactions serve a reader who is also away from home.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Exile', BrightWeavings
claims.quote: their observations and reactions become a way in for the reader

claims.claim: Kay says the idea of exile lets a novelist underscore elements of the society being evoked by asking why people are exiled, what it means for them and for those left behind.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Exile', BrightWeavings
claims.quote: underscore elements of the society being evoked
claims.page: body, on exile as a technique

claims.claim: Kay says he does not write novels inspired by history to offer easy parallels to our own time, because that can feel lazy or glib or both.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Exile', BrightWeavings
claims.quote: That can feel lazy, or glib, or both

claims.claim: Kay praises Penelope Fitzgerald's short novels for achieving so much with such small strokes that they frequently feel miraculous.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, '6 Books I Love', cbc.ca
claims.quote: achieve so much with such small strokes

claims.feature: other: not talking down to the reader
claims.claim: Kay praises Dorothy Dunnett for flatly refusing to talk down to her readers, making demands and rewarding them.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, '6 Books I Love', cbc.ca
claims.quote: flatly refuses to talk down to her readers

claims.feature: other: quarter turn to the fantastic
claims.claim: Kay tells The Guardian he steeps himself in a period and then twists it just a little to give himself ethical and creative space.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, quoted by Alison Flood, The Guardian
claims.quote: I steep myself in a period and then I twist it just that little bit
claims.page: later in the article, on El Cid

claims.feature: other: quarter turn to the fantastic
claims.claim: Alison Flood reports that Kay loves one critic's description of his work as history with a quarter-turn to the fantastic; the phrase is the critic's, reported by Flood.
claims.source: Alison Flood (reporter's paraphrase), The Guardian
claims.quote: history with a quarter-turn to the fantastic

claims.claim: Kay says he has been calling the current practice an epidemic of co-opting real lives, while declining to criticise writers who do it.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, quoted by Alison Flood, The Guardian
claims.quote: an epidemic of co-opting real lives
